title: Lost in tabulation: Diverging US-China trade data point to tariff evasion
gist: China reported $258.1B of exports to the US in Jan–Jul 2026 versus $158.3B of US-recorded imports, a $99.8B gap (63% of US imports, ~5x the 2021–24 norm) that PIIE attributes mainly to tariff evasion via underinvoicing and relabeling (notably through Vietnam). As a result, US data overstate decoupling and tariff effectiveness; de minimis and Chinese rebate fraud are judged minor contributors.

insights.claim: From January through July 2026, the US Census Bureau recorded $158.3 billion in merchandise imports from China (incl. Hong Kong), while China reported $258.1 billion in exports to the US, a $99.8 billion gap equal to 63% of reported US imports.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Official US import data materially understate actual Chinese goods flowing to the US.
insights.quote: The $99.8 billion difference was equivalent to 63 percent of reported US imports from China.

insights.claim: The 2026 US-China reporting gap as a share of US imports is nearly five times its 2021–24 average of roughly 13%.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Signals a structural break in data reliability coinciding with the 2025 tariff hikes.
insights.quote: This share was nearly five times its 2021–24 average.

insights.claim: If the average monthly US-China trade data gap observed in January–July 2026 persists, the cumulative gap for full-year 2026 will exceed $170 billion.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Scale of potentially uncollected tariff revenue and mismeasured trade is very large.
insights.quote: If the average monthly gap observed from January through July persists for the rest of the year, the cumulative gap for 2026 will exceed $170 billion.

insights.claim: By July 2026, China-reported monthly exports to the US were only about 4% below their 2024 average, whereas US-reported imports from China were 26% below their 2024 average.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Real US-China trade decline is far smaller than US data suggest; Chinese export exposure to the US remains largely intact.

insights.claim: The reported decline in US imports from China should not be treated as a clean measure of economic decoupling or of US tariff effectiveness, because US bilateral import data have become less reliable.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Decoupling narratives built on US customs data overstate the shift away from China.
insights.quote: The reported decline in US imports from China should not be treated as a clean measure of either economic decoupling or the effectiveness of US tariffs.

insights.claim: The US-China trade data gap was historically negative before 2020 (US reported more imports than China reported exports), reversed in 2020, and averaged about 13% of US imports during 2021–24.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Provides the baseline against which the current anomaly is measured.

insights.claim: In 2025 the average effective US tariff rate on imports from China and Hong Kong was 30%, and it remained at 24% in 2026 through July versus a 6% average effective rate on imports from other countries.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: A large tariff differential versus other origins creates strong incentives for origin fraud and underinvoicing.
insights.quote: In 2025, the average effective tariff rate on US merchandise imports from China and Hong Kong was 30 percent.

insights.claim: Tariff evasion appears to be the most likely explanation for the recent growth in the US-China trade reporting gap, though the exact causes remain uncertain.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Implies effective tariff collection and enforcement are weaker than headline rates suggest.
insights.quote: Still, tariff evasion appears the most likely explanation for its recent growth.

insights.claim: Federal Reserve researchers estimated that tariff evasion accounted for about $55 billion of the $88 billion shift in the US-China reporting gap between 2018 and 2020, and the 2025 tariffs were substantially higher and broader than the 2018–20 measures.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests evasion scales with tariff intensity, so the 2025 regime likely spurred more of it.

insights.claim: Tariff evasion methods include misstating country of origin, reclassifying goods across product categories with different rates, and understating declared value or quantity; because export and import declarations are filed separately, underinvoicing creates a gap between them.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Explains why trade data divergences are a usable signal of evasion.
insights.locator: Tariff evasion can take several forms.

insights.claim: A New York Times analysis found the average value of merchandise per shipping container from China fell by around 40% between January 2025 and February 2026, consistent with underinvoicing.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Per-container value is an alternative indicator of underinvoicing and tariff revenue leakage.
insights.quote: the average value of merchandise per shipping container from China fell by around 40 percent between January 2025 and February 2026
insights.locator: Tariff evasion can take several forms.

insights.claim: A Nikkei Asia investigation describes allegations that logistics providers used shell companies as importers of record and manipulated invoices to reduce US duties, and some Chinese companies are reluctant to claim US tariff refunds for fear that scrutiny would expose irregular entries.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Points to enforcement and legal risk around importers of record and tariff refund claims.
insights.locator: Tariff evasion can take several forms.

insights.claim: False declarations of origin create a positive data gap for the true origin country and an offsetting negative gap for the false origin country; Vietnam's gap with the US runs opposite to China's.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Mirror-image gaps in third countries can be used to track transshipment.
insights.locator: The effects of tariff evasion are not confined

insights.claim: From January through July 2026, the US recorded $149.6 billion in imports from Vietnam while Vietnam reported $105.0 billion in exports to the US, a $44.6 billion discrepancy consistent with Chinese goods being relabeled as Vietnamese.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Part of reported US imports from Vietnam is likely Chinese content, overstating supply-chain diversification.
insights.quote: The resulting $44.6 billion discrepancy is consistent with some Chinese goods being relabeled as Vietnamese
insights.locator: The effects of tariff evasion are not confined

insights.claim: After subtracting the 2021–24 average gap, the cumulative adjusted gap through July 2026 is $109.7 billion for China and Hong Kong and negative $62.5 billion for Vietnam; if Vietnam's gap were entirely relabeled Chinese exports, relabeling would explain 57% of the adjusted US-China gap.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Vietnam transshipment may be the single largest evasion channel, a target for future US enforcement.
insights.quote: such relabeling would account for 57 percent of the adjusted US-China gap

insights.claim: The US de minimis exemption ($800 duty-free) contributed to the gap's emergence in 2020, with Chinese low-value e-commerce exports to the US rising from $1.4 billion in 2018 to $22.9 billion in 2024, but its end for China in May 2025 and global suspension that August should have narrowed the gap.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Rules out e-commerce parcels as the driver of the recent gap, strengthening the evasion thesis.
insights.locator: Other developments have contributed to the gap

insights.claim: The value of global imports entering the US under the de minimis exemption fell 26% in fiscal year 2025, and US low-value import data from China show a structural break in May 2025 that likely reflects improved coverage rather than growth in low-value trade.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Changes in US data collection can distort trend readings in import statistics.

insights.claim: Chinese export-rebate fraud explained about $12 billion of the 2018–20 gap shift, but is unlikely to drive the recent gap because China cut export rebates from December 2024 and again in January 2026 and has inspected more than 130,000 firms suspected of fraudulent invoicing since 2024.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: China's fiscal tightening on exporters reduces incentives to overstate exports, isolating US-side evasion.
insights.quote: inspecting more than 130,000 firms suspected of fraudulent invoicing
insights.locator: A second possible cause of the US-China

insights.claim: Discriminatory bilateral tariffs can redirect trade through third countries without substantially reducing US reliance on Chinese content or China's role in global production.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Tariff-driven reshoring and decoupling bets may disappoint as Chinese content persists via third countries.
insights.quote: the episode illustrates the limits of using discriminatory tariffs to address bilateral trade imbalances

insights.claim: Systematic sharing and matching of transaction-level customs data between the US and China could help counter tariff evasion and tax fraud; a cooperation framework exists but implementation appears limited.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Better data matching would raise effective tariff collection and could tighten enforcement on transshippers.

insights.claim: Addressing US-China trade imbalances requires domestic adjustment: the US must rein in large fiscal deficits that feed its trade deficit, while China must stimulate domestic consumption and reduce industrial overcapacity.
insights.speaker: Gregory Auclair
insights.so_what: Imbalances persist absent fiscal consolidation in the US and rebalancing in China, regardless of tariffs.
insights.quote: The United States needs to rein in its large fiscal deficits, which contribute to its trade deficit, while China needs to stimulate domestic consumption and reduce industrial overcapacity.
